subject: math
title: Ray
summary: A ray has one endpoint and extends forever in one direction — like a laser beam. Explore how rays are named, how they differ from lines and segments, and how two rays make an angle.

crossReferences.label: Line (Geometry)
crossReferences.note: A ray is part of a line — cut the line at one point and keep going one way.

crossReferences.label: Segment (Geometry)
crossReferences.note: A segment stops at both ends; a ray stops at only one.

crossReferences.label: Angle (Geometry)
crossReferences.note: Two rays sharing an endpoint form an angle.

compareCandidate.label: Ray vs. line
compareCandidate.description: A line extends forever in BOTH directions; a ray has one endpoint and extends forever in only ONE direction.

processes: Making an angle with two rays
plainLanguageExplanation: A ray is a straight path with one endpoint and one infinite direction. Start at the endpoint, go straight, and never stop — like a flashlight beam. You draw a ray with a dot at the endpoint and an arrowhead at the other end. To name it, the endpoint comes FIRST: ray AB starts at A and passes through B. Two rays that share their endpoint make an angle — the shared endpoint is called the vertex.

keyFacts.label: Definition

keyFacts.label: Two rays

keyFacts.label: Endpoint
keyFacts.value: Also called the vertex in an angle

whyItMatters: Rays model real one-way motion — sunlight, laser pointers, and light beams. They are also the arms of every angle, so understanding rays unlocks angle geometry.
didYouKnow: Sunlight reaching Earth is modeled as rays from the sun — that is why light drawings use arrowheads, showing the light keeps traveling in one direction.
compareReason: Students mix up rays and lines — comparing shows the single endpoint and single direction that define a ray.
